definition: Japanese chess — a harder variant than Western chess tackled by AlphaZero, which matched top engines shortly after Go and chess.
details: Japanese chess — a harder variant than Western chess tackled by AlphaZero, which matched top engines shortly after Go and chess.

explainer.lead: Shogi, or Japanese chess, is a demanding test of decision-making: a player must repeatedly choose strong moves in a game considered harder than Western chess. It matters to AI because AlphaZero took on shogi after Go and chess and soon matched top shogi engines.

tiers.eli5: Shogi is like a particularly difficult chess puzzle where every turn asks, “Which move gives me the best chance to win?” A computer has to make that choice again and again as the game changes. AlphaZero learned to play well enough to match the best shogi engines, after already tackling Go and chess.
tiers.practitioner: For an engineer, shogi is a demanding setting for evaluating game-playing systems, with performance judged against strong engines. AlphaZero is the named example: it matched top shogi engines shortly after its Go and chess results. Avoid assuming that success in one board game transfers automatically to another, or that matching top engines means finding a provably optimal move in every position.
tiers.paperLevel: Play can be represented as a sequence of states s and actions a: at each state, select a in A(s) to maximize the expected final game result. Shogi is the Japanese-chess instance of this decision problem, described as harder than Western chess; AlphaZero matched top engines shortly after its Go and chess results. This establishes engine-level performance, not a closed-form optimal solution for every shogi position.

explainer.example: Give AlphaZero a shogi position and let it choose moves as the game unfolds. Its resulting playing strength can then be compared with top shogi engines; AlphaZero matched them shortly after tackling Go and chess.

explainer.intuition: Each turn is an optimization problem: choose the move most likely to lead to a good final outcome. Shogi makes that repeated choice especially demanding, so strong play is a meaningful test for a general game-playing system.
howItWorks: Start with the current shogi position.
Choose a move aimed at improving the chance of winning.
Continue making decisions as the position changes.
Assess playing strength against top shogi engines.
explainer.whyItMatters: Shogi provides a harder test than Western chess for systems that must make a long sequence of consequential choices. AlphaZero’s result showed that its strong game play extended beyond Go and chess.
misconceptions: Shogi was not AlphaZero’s first board-game challenge; it followed Go and chess.
Matching top engines does not prove optimal play in every position.
Strong shogi play does not automatically imply success at every optimization problem.
